name: sumy
purpose: Classical extractive summarisation library implementing LexRank, LSA, TextRank, Luhn, SumBasic and KL-divergence summarisers for plain text in many languages.
journalism_use_case: Rapid triage of long documents where every summary sentence must be verbatim from the original: a 300-page inquiry report reduced to twenty of its own sentences, which a reporter can trust as quoted text rather than having to re-verify against a generative paraphrase.
pros: Extractive by construction, so it cannot hallucinate — the single most important safety property for summarisation in journalism, and the reason to prefer it over an LLM for triage
No models, no GPU, no network: an afternoon's integration with no infrastructure and no privacy surface
Multiple algorithms let you compare outputs cheaply and pick one that suits your document type
Stable and still released (v0.13.0, 2026-08-12) after many years; Apache-2.0
cons: Extractive summaries read disjointedly — useful for triage, unusable as published prose
Quality drops sharply on short documents and on highly structured material such as spreadsheets, email headers or forms, which are common in leaks
Sentence selection is frequency-driven, so it favours repetitive boilerplate and can miss the one anomalous sentence that is the actual story
NLTK data dependency for tokenisation and stemming is a small but annoying extra download step
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 3,701 stars with only 7 open issues — a finished library with minimal support burden, released 2026-08-12 and pushed 2026-11-11.
assessment: A sensible, boring choice that I would use deliberately in place of an LLM for first-pass document triage, precisely because its failure mode is 'unhelpful' rather than 'confidently invented'. For your profile the pattern worth building is: sumy for a verbatim extract shown to the reporter, with the full document one click away — never an abstractive summary presented as the document's content.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-11, latest release v0.13.0 (2026-08-12), 3,701 stars, 7 open issues. Low change velocity with a current release and essentially no backlog — the textbook profile of a complete, maintained library rather than a declining one.
costs: No fee, negligible compute, no paid dependencies.
privacy: Fully local, no model downloads beyond NLTK corpora, no network at runtime.
alternatives: BERTopic for thematic rather than per-document triage
txtai if you want semantic search plus optional abstractive summarisation in one stack
A self-hosted LLM for abstractive summaries — accepting hallucination risk and a mandatory verification step

name: Surya
purpose: Document OCR model suite covering text detection and recognition in 90+ languages, layout analysis, reading-order detection, table structure recognition and LaTeX/maths OCR.
journalism_use_case: High-accuracy local alternative to commercial document AI for messy multi-column reports, forms and financial tables — the model layer that makes Marker's output good, usable directly when you want the structured layout data rather than Markdown.
pros: Accuracy on complex layouts is at the top of the open field, materially better than Tesseract on multi-column and tabular material
Covers detection, recognition, layout, reading order and table structure in one model family, so you are not stitching four research repos together
Extremely active (v0.24.0, 2026-11-13) with a remarkably clean tracker — 2 open issues against 21,599 stars
Runs entirely locally on your own GPU, so documents never reach a vendor
cons: Code is Apache-2.0 but the WEIGHTS are not open source: the README badge labels them OpenRAIL-M and links to datalab.to/pricing, where commercial use requires a licence above $5M in revenue OR funding — not an OSI licence and a real compliance decision
The auto-spawned inference server can be pointed at a remote OpenAI-compatible endpoint, which is an exfiltration path that must be explicitly closed when handling source material
GPU needed for real throughput; CPU inference is impractical for corpus-scale work
As a model suite rather than a tool, you must write the orchestration — or use Marker, which inherits the same licence question
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Checkable facts: 21,599 stars with 2 open issues (exceptional triage); and the vendor pricing page stating the threshold verbatim — '$5M for Marker and Surya' — verified 2026-11-16 and recorded in sources/recovered/cat/pricing.tsv.
assessment: Technically excellent and licence-constrained in exactly the same way as Marker. My recommendation for your profile: if you are under the revenue/funding threshold, use Marker (which wraps Surya) rather than Surya directly, unless you specifically need the layout JSON. If you are over the threshold or cannot be certain, use Docling instead and accept a modest accuracy cost. Either way, pin the inference server to localhost so the remote-endpoint option cannot be triggered by configuration drift.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-13, latest release v0.24.0 published the same day, 21,599 stars, 2 open issues. Same-day push and release with near-zero backlog; commercially backed by Datalab.
model_or_data_licence: OpenRAIL-M for the weights (README 'Model License: OpenRAIL-M' linking to datalab.to/pricing). NOT OSI-approved. Commercial use above $5M revenue OR funding requires a paid licence.
licence_restrictions: Revenue/funding threshold on weights; OpenRAIL-M additionally imposes use-based behavioural restrictions that flow downstream on redistribution. The Apache-2.0 code licence does not cure this.
costs: Code free; weights free below the threshold, otherwise a commercial licence at a price not publicly listed (quote required). Datalab's hosted API is priced separately: Free $0 with a $20/$10 monthly allowance, Team $400/month, Enterprise custom (verified 2026-11-16, USD). Self-hosted: one GPU host.
privacy: Local inference; first-run weight download from HuggingFace. The material risk is the configurable remote inference endpoint — verify it points at localhost before processing source material.
alternatives: Marker for the full conversion pipeline over these same models
Docling where a clean permissive position on weights is required
PaddleOCR for CJK/Arabic with Apache-2.0 code (weights unverified)
blockers: Weights are OpenRAIL-M with a $5M revenue-or-funding commercial threshold

name: Tabula
maintainer: Tabula / Manuel Aristarán, Mike Tigas, Jeremy Merrill (OpenNews lineage)
purpose: Desktop application (served as a local web UI) that lets a user draw selection boxes around tables in a PDF and export them as CSV, TSV or JSON.
journalism_use_case: The canonical no-code newsroom tool: a reporter draws a box around a table in a PDF budget or disclosure filing and gets a CSV, with no engineer, no command line and no cloud service involved. For a one-off table in a document that matters today, this remains the fastest path from PDF to spreadsheet.
pros: Reporters can use it unaided, which is the entire point and is still unmatched for direct manual table extraction
Runs entirely on localhost with nothing uploaded, so it is safe for sensitive documents in a way that web-based PDF converters are not
Single Java download, no installation complexity, works offline
Long journalism lineage (OpenNews/Knight-Mozilla origin) and the libraries beneath it (tabula-java, tabula-py) remain active
cons: GUI development has largely stalled: last push 2025-03-14 and the latest release v1.2.1 dates from 2018-06-04, with 541 open issues — the clearest 'frozen tool' profile in this segment
Text-layer PDFs only; no OCR, so scans need OCRmyPDF first and reporters will not know why it 'does not work'
Manual selection does not scale beyond a handful of documents — there is no batch mode in the GUI
Java runtime dependency is increasingly awkward on managed newsroom laptops
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The documented evidence is the maintenance gap itself: 7,496 stars, 541 open issues, last push March 2025, last release June 2018. The project's own ecosystem has shifted to tabula-java and tabula-py, which remain usable — so this is a GUI that has stopped evolving rather than a dead capability.
assessment: Still worth keeping on reporters' machines because the capability is real and the alternative for a non-coder is manual retyping. But I would not treat it as a maintained tool: no releases in over seven years and 541 open issues means any bug you hit is permanent. For anything repeatable, move to Camelot or pdfplumber in a pipeline. If a newsroom standardises on it, accept that it is frozen software being used because it still works.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2025-03-14, latest release v1.2.1 (2018-06-04), 7,496 stars, 541 open issues. No release for over seven years, no push for twenty months, and a very large backlog. Classified dormant rather than archived because no deprecation notice exists and the underlying libraries (tabula-java/tabula-py) are maintained separately; the GUI itself is not being developed.
costs: Free. Requires a Java runtime. No infrastructure.
privacy: Fully local — the UI is served from localhost and nothing is uploaded. This remains its strongest property and the reason to prefer it over any web-based PDF-to-CSV service.
alternatives: Camelot for scripted extraction with confidence scores
pdfplumber for coordinate-level control and auditable extraction
tabula-py / tabula-java — the maintained libraries from the same lineage, usable in a pipeline
blockers: No release since 2018 and 541 open issues — frozen GUI; use the maintained libraries for anything new

name: Tesseract OCR
purpose: LSTM line-recognition OCR engine for 100+ languages with a CLI and the libtesseract C/C++ API, outputting text, hOCR, ALTO, TSV and searchable PDF, and trainable for new scripts.
journalism_use_case: Baseline fully offline OCR for scanned court filings, FOIA releases and paper archives — and more importantly, the engine underneath OCRmyPDF, Tika, ICIJ extract and Datashare, so its behaviour determines the text quality of most document pipelines you will build.
pros: The de facto standard: understanding Tesseract's behaviour means understanding the text quality of almost every open document pipeline, because they all wrap it
Fully offline with 100+ language packs, CPU-only, and packaged in every distro — effectively zero friction to deploy anywhere, including air-gapped
Apache-2.0 for both the engine and the tessdata traineddata from the same project, so there is no licence complication
Still actively released (5.5.4, 2026-10-28) after decades, with 77,561 stars and a managed backlog
cons: Weak on handwriting and badly degraded scans — the ceiling that drives teams to Surya, Kraken or commercial OCR, and no amount of preprocessing removes it
No layout or table-structure output beyond hOCR bounding boxes, so structure must come from another stage
Per-language quality varies a lot, and the 'best' versus 'fast' traineddata choice materially changes both accuracy and runtime in ways that are not obvious
490 open issues; the project is maintained but changes slowly, and accuracy improvements come from newer neural OCR elsewhere
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The adoption evidence is structural and verifiable from dependency declarations: OCRmyPDF, Apache Tika's OCR path, ICIJ extract, Datashare and Paperless-ngx all use Tesseract. 77,561 stars with 490 open issues and a release on 2026-10-28.
assessment: Adopt by default, via OCRmyPDF rather than directly — the wrapper handles the preprocessing and PDF assembly you would otherwise write badly. For your profile the key judgement is knowing when to escalate: if Tesseract's output on a corpus is poor, no tuning will fix handwriting or heavy degradation, and the right move is Kraken (handwriting) or Surya/Marker (complex print) for that subset rather than more preprocessing.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-15, latest release 5.5.4 (2026-10-28), 77,561 stars, 490 open issues. Current commits and point releases on the 5.x line from a community team; long-term stability is the defining characteristic.
model_or_data_licence: Apache-2.0 for tessdata traineddata from the same project (verify per language pack, since some community-contributed packs differ).
costs: No fee. CPU-only; OCR time is roughly linear in page count. Language packs are small. Among the cheapest capabilities in the catalogue.
privacy: Fully local with no network at inference. Language-pack downloads are the only external fetch and can be pre-staged.
alternatives: OCRmyPDF as the wrapper you should actually use
Surya/Marker where print accuracy is the constraint
Kraken for handwriting; PaddleOCR for CJK and Arabic

name: txtai
purpose: All-in-one embeddings database and workflow framework combining vector search, sparse/hybrid search, graph components, pipelines for summarisation and transcription, and an API server.
journalism_use_case: A single dependency that gives a small newsroom semantic search, clustering and summarisation over an extracted corpus without assembling four separate systems — the pragmatic answer when there is no engineering team to integrate sentence-transformers, FAISS, a search API and a UI.
pros: Breadth per unit of integration effort is the selling point: index, hybrid search, graph and pipelines in one package, which suits a one-engineer newsroom
Hybrid sparse-plus-dense search addresses semantic search's recall problem better than pure vector search, which matters when you must evidence completeness
Very actively developed (v9.14.0, 2026-10-06) with an exceptionally clean tracker (40 open issues against 13,555 stars)
Apache-2.0 with a local-first default and an embeddable API server
cons: Breadth means you inherit opinions: the pipeline abstractions are convenient until you need something slightly different, at which point assembling the components yourself would have been simpler
GPU recommended for embedding large corpora; CPU indexing of a leak-scale corpus is slow
If LLM summarisation pipelines are enabled, outputs can hallucinate and must never be quoted without checking the source document — the framework makes this easy to enable and easy to forget
Model licences depend entirely on what you select and were not individually verified
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 13,555 stars with 40 open issues and a release on 2026-10-06 — a strong issue-throughput signal for a framework of this scope. No journalism deployment verified.
assessment: A good fit for your profile specifically where time-to-capability matters more than architectural control: it collapses a week of integration into a day. I would use it for an internal research index over an already-extracted corpus, with local models only and LLM pipelines disabled by default. For a long-lived flagship archive I would still prefer explicit components (Solr or OpenSearch plus sentence-transformers) because you will eventually need to control each layer.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v9.14.0 (2026-10-06), 13,555 stars, 40 open issues. High release cadence on a 9.x line with a very small backlog.
model_or_data_licence: Varies by the model selected; not individually verified.
licence_restrictions: Code unrestricted. Licence risk is imported with whichever embedding or LLM model you configure.
costs: No fee. GPU recommended for bulk embedding; FAISS/HNSW indexes are local files. If you configure a hosted LLM provider you incur its token charges — not priced here. Estimate.
privacy: Fully local with local models. The configuration risk is explicit: pointing it at hosted LLM or embedding providers sends document text off-site. Review the configuration before processing source material.
alternatives: sentence-transformers plus FAISS for explicit control
Datasette where the corpus is structured rather than textual
Apache Solr or OpenSearch for full-document scale with mature operations

name: uroman
purpose: Universal romaniser that converts text in virtually any script to the Latin alphabet using rule tables, with no trained model and no language specification required.
journalism_use_case: Makes non-Latin-script corpora searchable and joinable: romanise Arabic, Cyrillic, Devanagari, Thai or Chinese names so a sanctions list, a corporate registry and a leaked ledger can be fuzzy-matched in one Latin-script index — the step that makes cross-script name matching possible at all.
pros: Script-agnostic with no language detection required, so it handles a mixed-script corpus without routing logic — a genuine simplification
Rule-based and deterministic: the same input always romanises identically, which is what a reproducible matching pipeline needs
No models, no dependencies of consequence, entirely offline — trivially deployable on an evidence machine
Covers an unusually wide range of scripts for a single tool, including ones with little other tooling
cons: Romanisation is lossy and irreversible: distinct names can collide, which creates false matches that must be adjudicated
Output follows no single standard scheme (not ALA-LC, not BGN/PCGN), so it is a matching aid rather than a citable rendering — never use uroman output as a published name spelling

Licence carries a non-standard condition: the LICENSE.txt grants MIT-equivalent rights but states that 'Any publication of projects using uroman shall acknowledge its use', so it is not a clean SPDX identifier (GitHub reports NOASSERTION)
Dormant: last push 2024-07-26 with release v1.3.1 (2024-06-28) and 17 open issues
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the acknowledgement clause read directly from LICENSE.txt in session 1 and retained; last push 2024-07-26; 258 stars. uroman is a well-cited research tool in MT and cross-lingual IR, which is adjacent-field credibility rather than journalism evidence.
assessment: Use it as a matching-key generator, never as a name renderer, and remember the acknowledgement condition — for your work that means a line in the methodology note of any story whose matching depended on it, which is a trivial obligation but a real one. The dormancy is acceptable here because rule tables do not rot the way a dependency-heavy library does; the risk is that an unsupported script or a bug will never be fixed.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2024-07-26, latest release v1.3.1 (2024-06-28), 258 stars, 17 open issues. Over two years without activity. Classified dormant; mitigated by the nature of the tool — deterministic rule tables with no dependency surface degrade far more slowly than typical software.
licence: MIT-style permissive with an added acknowledgement condition (LICENSE.txt grants MIT-equivalent rights but states 'Any publication of projects using uroman shall acknowledge its use'; GitHub API reports NOASSERTION)
model_or_data_licence: n/a — rule tables, no trained weights.
licence_restrictions: Acknowledgement is a publication obligation: any publication of a project using uroman must acknowledge it. Not a use restriction, but it must be tracked so the credit actually appears.
costs: No fee, negligible resources, no paid dependencies.
privacy: Entirely local, no network, no models.
alternatives: rigour for corporate-name normalisation within Latin script
ICU transliteration for standards-conformant, citable transliteration schemes
Language-specific transliteration libraries where a published rendering is required

name: VisiData
purpose: Terminal spreadsheet and data-exploration tool that opens dozens of formats (CSV, JSON, SQLite, Parquet, XLSX, HTML tables and more), with frequency analysis, filtering, reshaping, joins and a replayable command log.
journalism_use_case: First-look tool on a messy leaked dataset: profile a 10-million-row CSV, spot encoding and type breakage, and build a cleaning recipe — all over SSH on an air-gapped evidence machine where no GUI is available. That last property is why it is in this catalogue rather than a general data tool.
pros: Works over SSH on a headless evidence machine, which is exactly where sensitive data should be processed and where OpenRefine cannot go
Frequency-table-first workflow surfaces data-quality problems (stray encodings, impossible dates, duplicate keys) in seconds rather than after an hour of pandas
The command log is replayable, so an exploration session becomes a reproducible script — a real methodology asset
Handles very large files without loading everything into memory, unlike OpenRefine's JVM heap limits
cons: Steep keyboard-driven learning curve; a reporter will not pick it up unaided, so it is an analyst/engineer tool despite being an 'application'
GPL-3.0 affects redistribution inside proprietary tooling (irrelevant for internal use)
Exploration and reshaping rather than probabilistic linkage — pair it with Splink or dedupe for matching work
Terminal rendering of wide tables is cramped; some data shapes are genuinely easier to see in a GUI
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 9,473 stars with only 8 open issues and a release v3.5 (2026-10-28) — excellent issue throughput. VisiData is a well-known tool in the data-journalism community, reflected in its documentation and conference presence; no specific deployment verified.
assessment: Adopt it for anyone on your team who works in a terminal, specifically because it is the only serious data-exploration tool that works well on a locked-down headless box. The pairing I would standardise: VisiData for profiling and cleaning recipes on the evidence machine, Datasette for sharing the result with reporters, Splink when linkage is needed. The learning curve is real but one afternoon gets an analyst productive.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-11, latest release v3.5 (2026-10-28), 9,473 stars, 8 open issues. Recent release and a near-empty backlog from a long-standing single maintainer.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0: redistribution of a modified version obliges source release. Internal newsroom use is unaffected.
costs: No fee. Runs anywhere Python runs, including a small VM. Optional per-format loader libraries. Negligible cost.
privacy: Fully local with no network calls, and usable over SSH on an isolated machine — a deliberate privacy advantage over GUI tools that require the data on a workstation.
alternatives: OpenRefine for a GUI-based, reporter-accessible workflow
Datasette for sharing and browsing rather than cleaning
DuckDB plus a notebook for heavier analytical work

name: Whisper
purpose: Encoder-decoder speech model trained on 680,000 hours of multilingual audio, performing transcription, language identification and speech translation, released with MIT code and MIT weights.
journalism_use_case: Baseline transcription of interviews and leaked audio where model provenance matters, and the canonical implementation that nearly every newsroom transcription tool wraps — so its documented failure modes are the failure modes you will encounter whichever wrapper you deploy.
pros: MIT weights as well as MIT code — a genuinely unrestricted model, which is rare and removes every commercial-publication concern
Multilingual performance across many languages from a single model, so one deployment covers a cross-border newsroom
Reference status means every wrapper, benchmark and bug report in the ecosystem is interpretable against it
Still the baseline against which newer ASR is measured, so quality is well characterised rather than claimed
cons: Documented hallucination on silence and poor recordings is the critical journalism risk: Whisper can emit fluent, plausible, entirely invented sentences, which is far more dangerous than a garbled transcript
No speaker diarisation and only approximate word timestamps, so quote verification needs WhisperX or forced alignment
large-v3 needs roughly 10GB VRAM, and the reference implementation is much slower than faster-whisper or whisper.cpp for the same output
Repository has slowed: pushed 2026-08-31 with the last release v20250625 (2025-06-26) — OpenAI's attention is elsewhere, and the ecosystem forks are where development happens
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey, but Whisper's hallucination behaviour on silence and low-quality audio is a widely documented phenomenon discussed extensively in the project's issue tracker and in published evaluations — I am treating it as an established property of the model rather than an anecdote. 112,964 stars, 186 open issues.
assessment: Use the weights, not this implementation: faster-whisper or whisper.cpp give the same output far more efficiently. The operationally important point for your work is procedural rather than technical — any Whisper-derived transcript used for quotation must be checked against the audio at the quoted passage, because the model's failure mode is fluent invention. VAD preprocessing (which faster-whisper includes) materially reduces but does not eliminate this.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-08-31, latest release v20250625 (2025-06-26), 112,964 stars, 186 open issues. Nearly 17 months without a release and ~2.5 months since last push. Classified stable-low rather than declining because the artefact that matters — the weights — is final and unchanging, and the ecosystem maintains the tooling; but do not expect fixes from this repository.
licence_restrictions: None — unusually clean for a model of this capability.
costs: No fee. GPU with ~10GB VRAM for large-v3, or slow CPU inference. Note the separate OpenAI hosted Whisper API is a paid service under OpenAI's terms — a different thing from these weights, and inappropriate for sensitive audio.
privacy: Fully local inference after weight download; no audio leaves the machine. The confusion to guard against is between these local weights and OpenAI's hosted transcription API, which does transmit audio.
alternatives: faster-whisper for the same weights with much better throughput
whisper.cpp for CPU and field hardware
NVIDIA Parakeet (CC-BY-4.0) for higher English accuracy

name: whisper.cpp
purpose: Plain C/C++ implementation of Whisper inference using the ggml tensor library, with quantised GGUF models, no Python dependency, and backends for CPU, Metal, CUDA, Vulkan and OpenVINO.
journalism_use_case: Transcribing suspect audio and video locally so the words in a claimed 'leaked recording' can be checked, searched and quoted without uploading sensitive material to any service — and because it needs no Python, it runs on a hardened or borrowed machine where installing a toolchain is not an option.
pros: No Python and no dependency hell: a single binary plus a model file, which is the most deployable transcription stack here and the right choice for a locked-down or borrowed laptop
Quantised GGUF models run usably on ordinary CPUs and on Apple Silicon via Metal, removing the GPU requirement entirely
Extremely active (pushed 2026-11-17, release v1.9.5 2026-10-06) with 55,264 stars and a large but managed backlog
MIT code and MIT weights, so no licensing friction at all
cons: No built-in diarisation, so multi-speaker material needs a separate pipeline
Quantisation trades accuracy for speed in ways that are model- and language-dependent, and the trade-off is not well documented for minority languages
API churn across releases can break downstream wrappers — a recurring complaint given how many tools embed it (373 open issues)
Still inherits Whisper's hallucination behaviour; the runtime does not fix the model's failure mode
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 55,264 stars with 373 open issues and a release on 2026-10-06; whisper.cpp is embedded in Buzz, Subtitle Edit and numerous desktop tools, which is verifiable from those projects and is strong evidence of practical reliability.
assessment: The transcription runtime I would standardise on for anything that must run on arbitrary hardware — field laptops, hostile-environment machines, a reporter's borrowed computer. For server-side batch work faster-whisper is better. The combination of 'single binary, no network, MIT weights' is uniquely well matched to media-in-exile constraints, and it is worth packaging a known-good binary plus model internally so reporters never download anything at the moment of need.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v1.9.5 (2026-10-06), 55,264 stars, 373 open issues. Daily commits and regular releases; the backlog reflects the number of platforms and wrappers rather than neglect.
costs: No fee. Runs on existing CPUs; model files are a few hundred MB to a few GB. Effectively zero marginal cost, which is a significant advantage for a small newsroom.
privacy: Fully local; model files fetched once and then no network at all. The single most deployable privacy-preserving transcription option in the catalogue.
alternatives: faster-whisper for server-side batch throughput
Buzz for a GUI over this engine
sherpa-onnx for embedded and streaming use cases

name: WhisperX
purpose: Pipeline combining faster-whisper transcription, wav2vec2 forced alignment for word-level timestamps, VAD-based batching and pyannote speaker diarisation.
journalism_use_case: Producing quote-accurate, speaker-attributed transcripts of multi-party interviews and hearings where you must jump to the exact second a phrase was spoken to verify it — the combination that turns a machine transcript into something an editor can check line by line.
pros: Word-level timestamps from forced alignment are materially more accurate than Whisper's native estimates, which is what makes quote verification practical at scale
Bundles the three stages (transcribe, align, diarise) that every newsroom audio pipeline needs, saving substantial integration work
BSD-2-Clause and actively released (v3.8.6, 2026-05-25) with 25,401 stars
VAD-based batching gives a large throughput gain over sequential processing
cons: Heavy dependency stack (faster-whisper, pyannote.audio, torchaudio, ffmpeg) and ~10GB VRAM for large-v3 plus diarisation — the most demanding transcription option here
Diarisation inherits pyannote's weaknesses: it degrades on overlapping speech and telephone-band audio, which describes much covertly recorded material
Alignment-model coverage is uneven outside major languages, so word-level timing quality varies by language in a way that is easy to overlook
Obtaining diarisation weights requires accepting pyannote's HuggingFace gate, which discloses your identity to the model authors
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 25,401 stars, 219 open issues, last release v3.8.6 (2026-05-25) with commits through 2026-11-12. The HuggingFace gating requirement is documented on pyannote's model card and is the most commonly reported setup obstacle for this project.
assessment: The right choice for an engineer-run interview and hearing pipeline, and the one I would build on for any investigation where quotes must be verifiable to the second. For your profile: pre-fetch the pyannote weights centrally, pin the whole stack in a container because the dependency graph is fragile, and check alignment quality explicitly for each non-major language before trusting the timestamps editorially.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-12, latest release v3.8.6 (2026-05-25), 25,401 stars, 219 open issues. Current commits with a release about six months old; active but with a slower release cadence than its dependencies, so pinning matters.
model_or_data_licence: Mixed: Whisper MIT; wav2vec2 aligners vary by language; pyannote diarisation weights MIT but gated on HuggingFace.
licence_restrictions: No field-of-use restrictions found. The practical constraint is the pyannote access gate; check individual wav2vec2 aligner licences for less common languages.
costs: No fee. GPU with ~10GB VRAM recommended; CPU operation is impractical for the full pipeline. One GPU host serves a small newsroom's audio needs. Infrastructure estimate.
privacy: Local inference end to end; audio does not leave the machine. One-time external touchpoint is the gated pyannote weights download, best performed centrally.
alternatives: noScribe for a desktop application with the same capabilities for non-engineers
faster-whisper alone if speaker attribution is unnecessary
Montreal Forced Aligner for phone-level forensic alignment against a known transcript
blockers: Gated pyannote diarisation weights — plan a central download for air-gapped deployments

name: yente
purpose: Self-hostable entity-matching API that indexes OpenSanctions (or your own FollowTheMoney) data in Elasticsearch/OpenSearch and exposes search, match and OpenRefine-compatible reconciliation endpoints.
journalism_use_case: Screen a leaked client or shareholder list against sanctions and PEP data in bulk on your own infrastructure, then reconcile the same spreadsheet from OpenRefine — without the names ever leaving your network. That last property is the whole argument: using a hosted screening API would disclose your investigation's targets to a vendor.
pros: Solves a specific and serious operational-security problem: bulk screening without telling a third party who you are investigating
OpenRefine-compatible reconciliation endpoint means an analyst can reconcile a spreadsheet against sanctions data entirely in-house — the fix for OpenRefine's one privacy flaw
MIT licensed, actively released (v5.5.1, 2026-10-30), maintained by the organisation that produces the data
Returns scored candidates with the matching features, so adjudication is informed rather than binary
cons: The code is MIT but the data it exists to serve is CC-BY-NC-4.0: commercial use of OpenSanctions data requires a paid licence (quote required), which directly affects a commercially operated newsroom

assessment: Adopt it specifically to keep screening in-house — the privacy argument is decisive and this is the only tool here that delivers it. Then resolve the data licence separately and in writing: if your outlet is commercially operated, 'we are journalism so it is non-commercial' is not a defensible reading of CC-BY-NC, and you should price the OpenSanctions commercial licence before building a workflow on it. Using the data for reporting leads versus building a paid product are different positions and should be decided explicitly.
